title: Patience, fairness and the human condition

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: People love to catalogue the traits they think characteristic of their species. Some, such as language, are obvious. Others, such as patience and fairness are more subtle. These traits, however, did not spring into existence fully formed. They evolved – and to understand human evolution it would help to know the genetic underpinnings of these traits and the order in which they evolved. One way of looking at these questions is to compare people with their closest relatives, great apes such as chimpanzees. Another is to compare people with each other. Three recent studies which take one or other of these approaches have cast light on the evolution of both patience and fairness. It turns out that patience is older than fairness. And, although the propensity to be fair varies a good deal from person to person, that variation is rooted in genetics rather than culture.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The essence of patience is the ability to delay the gratification of an appetite in favour of a greater ultimate reward. Past tests of the degree to which animals other than people can delay their gratification have focused on birds and monkeys. Both groups postpone accepting a reward if a bigger reward is on offer, but only for a few seconds. Birds, however, are only remotely related to humans, and even among primates, monkeys are not as close as apes. In the journal Current Biology, Marc Hauser of Harvard University and his colleagues compare chimpanzees and humans directly. Both, it turns out, can demonstrate a high degree of patience. In fact chimpanzees are more patient than people. The human participants in Dr Hauser's experiment (or game) were allowed to choose a food, such as raisins or chocolate. The chimpanzees were simply offered grapes – which they usually like. Otherwise the experimental conditions were identical. The choice was between one unit immediately, and three after two minutes. Chimpanzees were nearly 4 times more likely to wait for the bigger portion than humans were. This suggests not only that the trait of patience predates the split between humans and chimpanzees some 4 million years ago, but that the trait seems more characteristic of chimpanzees than people.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: When it comes to fairness, though, it is a different story. Economic theory has contrived a species it calls Homo economicus – a rational 'maximizer' who grabs what he can for himself. But, curiously, he makes no appearance in the ultimatum game, a classic economics experiment. In the game, two players, a proposer and a responder, divide a reward. It could be a cake, or cash, or even a bunch of grapes, and it could be divided equally or unequally. The game is so named because the proposition is an ultimatum. The responder can either accept the division or reject it. If he rejects it, both players receive nothing. Homo economicus would accept any division in which his share was not zero. But that is not what happens. Scores of studies have run the ultimatum game on human being across cultures and ages. Universally, people reject any share lower than 20% – apparently to punish the greed of the proposer. People do not act like Homo economicus. Instead they are the arbiters of fairness.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: To find out if chimpanzees share this sense of fairness, Keith Jensen and his colleagues at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig designed a way for chimpanzees to play the ultimatum game using dried fruit, usually raisins. The results as reported in Science, are the chimpanzees are simply rational maximizers. Though chimpanzee proposers consistently chose the highest number of raisins for themselves, responder chimpanzees did not reject even the meanest amounts for themselves. This is a telling outcome. A number of researchers in the field of human evolution think that a sense of patience – and a willingness to punish the unfair even at some cost to oneself – is one of humanity's most important of characteristics. It is what allows social groups to form and exhibit collaborative behaviour. Dr Jensen's data add weigh to the theory that his sophisticated idea of fair shares appeared in the hominid line only after the ancestors of chimpanzees and humans split from one another.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nor, according to the third of this convenient trilogy of studies, is a sense of fairness rooted in culture. Rather, it is genetic – as it would have to be in order to evolve. Paradoxically, discovering this relies on the fact that not everyone possesses it to the same degree. As they write in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Bjorn Wallace of the Stockholm School of Economics and his colleagues have shown this by playing the ultimatum game with human twins. They used the classic trick of neutralizing the effect of upbringing and exposing that of genetics by comparing identical twins (who share all their genes) with fraternal twins (who share half). Each twin of a pair played the ultimatum game with pieces of cake, both as proposer and as responder. Dr Wallace found, in the case of identical twins, a striking correlation between the average division that each member of a pair proposed and also between what they were unwilling to accept. In other words, their senses of what was fair were similar. No such correlations were seen in the behaviour of fraternal twins.
